objectives: Secure a negotiated settlement with the UK that avoids UK withdrawal of substantially equivalent concessions, protecting the EU-UK TCA relationship.
Preserve the EU's ability to conclude the domestic legislation and TRQ regime on schedule for the June Council vote.

Obtain UK acceptance of a country-specific or otherwise structured UK share of the TRQ (rather than pure global FCFS) that is politically saleable to the UK as 'compensation', without conceding so much volume/duty-free access that steel-producing member states in Council object.
Prevent the UK from joining a joint dispute or coordinated FTA-disapplication retaliation with Japan/Korea by giving the UK enough to see this process as distinct and separately resolved.
Keep the FTA-disapplication provision framed narrowly enough (or offer some carve-out/phase-in for the UK) that it doesn't become a rallying point for third parties.
Manage the interaction with the UK's own steel safeguard and its treatment of EU exporters, seeking reciprocal favourable treatment for EU-origin steel under the UK measure as part of any package.
Maintain EU credibility and standing as a reliable, good-faith Article XXVIII negotiating partner for future Geneva files, including with Turkey, Korea, India, Japan who are watching this precedent.
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement inside four rounds that gives the UK a defined, workable share of the TRQ (or equivalent compensation) sufficient that ministers accept it and do not withdraw concessions or join third-country retaliation, while the package remains within a mandate Council can approve without reopening it. It should also avoid setting a precedent that invites maximalist demands from Turkey/Korea/India/Japan. Failure: no deal, UK withdraws equivalent concessions, UK aligns with Japan/Korea in a joint dispute or FTA retaliation, or the settlement is generous enough that other principal suppliers demand parity that unpicks the EU's overall steel measure design or the Council mandate.
declaration.approach: Open by listening carefully to the UK's actual red lines before showing flexibility, since I have no fixed settlement figure from Brussels and need to calibrate. Signal early that the EU is willing to discuss a UK-specific quota share, a review clause, and possibly a carve-out or transitional treatment on the FTA-disapplication point, since these cost the EU relatively little relative to their political value to the UK, while holding the overall TRQ volume and out-of-quota rate closer to the EU's line as the harder-fought items. Use the FTA-disapplication issue and the UK's own safeguard treatment of EU exporters as linked bargaining chips — offer to soften disapplication or support favourable UK-measure treatment for EU exports in exchange for the UK not escalating with Japan/Korea and not pursuing full withdrawal rights. Keep language at the table measured and non-committal on numbers, reserving specific figures for capital consultation, since Phase 1 statements are visible to the UK and could be read back to Tokyo/Seoul. Aim to bank an agreement in principle by round 2-3, leaving round 4 as a buffer to close details, since Brussels needs time to secure Council approval before June. Throughout, treat the UK Geneva counterpart as a continuing partner across other Goods files, not a one-off adversary, to preserve working trust.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A guaranteed, meaningful UK-specific share of the TRQ (not global FCFS where Turkey/Korea's larger volumes crowd them out), preservation of current tariff-free volumes as close as possible, removal or softening of the FTA-disapplication clause, a review/sunset clause, and reciprocal good treatment for UK steel under the TCA. They also want to avoid being seen at home as having failed to protect the steel sector, and have leverage via their own Article XXVIII/safeguard process affecting EU exporters.

A durable legal footing for the steel TRQ regime that addresses non-market-economy overcapacity, minimal erosion of the 50%/400,000t global design, protection of EU steel producers' interests (favouring member states with production), but also awareness from steel-consuming member states not to overly restrict input supply, and a clean, timely conclusion before the June Council vote without setting a precedent that invites excessive demands from Turkey, Korea, India, Japan.

To use the EU's FTA-disapplication precedent and the UK's grievance as leverage to protect their own FTA preferences, potentially recruiting the UK into a joint dispute or coordinated retaliation to increase pressure on the EU across all four parallel Article XXVIII claims.

parties.who: Turkey and Korea (as principal suppliers in this same steel Article XXVIII process)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A large share of any TRQ given their bigger volumes; they will resist any UK-specific carve-out that reduces the global pool available to them, and will watch this negotiation closely as a precedent for their own parallel claims.

To preserve substantial interest consultation rights and watch for precedent on allocation methodology that could affect its own claim, likely favouring global/non-discriminatory allocation over country-specific carve-outs that disadvantage it.

objectives: Secure UK agreement to the modification within the four-round window so the Council can vote in June

Preserve a country-specific UK share within the TRQ rather than pure global first-come-first-served, but keep the aggregate quota volume tight enough to deliver a real reduction in tariff-free imports
Avoid setting a precedent with the UK settlement that Turkey/Korea (larger volumes) could leverage to demand disproportionately more
Retain the FTA-disapplication mechanism in substance, using it as a lever rather than a giveaway — trade it for UK movement on TCA-related asks, not abandon it for free
Get UK movement on EU exporters' treatment under the UK's own parallel safeguard/Article XXVIII process, so this is a package that helps EU steel producers on both sides
Keep a review clause narrow (e.g. mid-term technical review, not a reopening of volumes) so the regime's operation isn't destabilised a year in
Manage member state and industry optics: show a visible, defensible reduction in imports, not a rollover of the status quo
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement inside four rounds that (a) the Council can vote on in June, (b) delivers a materially lower tariff-free volume than current UK trade (2.4mt), (c) gives the UK enough (a specific share, a workable out-of-quota rate, reasonable duration, some reciprocity on the UK's own measure) that it doesn't trigger retaliation or become a rallying point for Turkey/Korea to demand more, and (d) does not require unwinding the FTA-disapplication provision entirely. Failure: no deal (process slips past June, Council vote delayed, UK retaliation risk crystallises in six months, and I've failed my instruction to preserve the regime's operation), or a deal so generous on volume/country share that it undermines the import-reduction objective and invites the same ask from Turkey and Korea, or a deal that requires abandoning provisions I was instructed to preserve.
declaration.approach: Open with the notified terms as the anchor but signal early that a UK-specific quota share and a review clause are negotiable — this is the cheapest compensation I can offer since it costs little against the aggregate cap while giving the UK seat something concrete to bring to capital. Hold firm longer on the out-of-quota rate and on the FTA-disapplication clause, since those matter most for the regime's long-term integrity and for not opening a precedent other claimants exploit. Use the parallel UK safeguard file as a bargaining chit: offer to discuss EU exporters' treatment under the UK measure as part of the package, making this look like a mutual de-escalation rather than a one-sided EU concession. Move in stages across the four rounds — concede on allocation method and quota share before I concede on rate or duration — so that if the UK is going to accept, they accept with the harder items last, and if they're not going to accept, I find that out before giving away the valuable concessions. Keep half an eye on the US retaliation threat and the Turkey/Korea comparison throughout: don't let the UK settlement look so favourable that it becomes the template others cite, and don't let the total package cost more than the political value of closing this by June.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A country-specific UK share of the TRQ well above a pure global pool, a lower out-of-quota rate or longer phase-in, exemption or carve-out for products where UK exports are concentrated, retention of TCA-based access or at least non-disapplication of preferences for the UK specifically, a review clause, and reciprocal protection for UK exporters under their own safeguard given the mirrored pressure on their industry. They will be under domestic pressure to show they defended UK steel jobs and may prefer a modest deal now over a damaging no-deal that delays their own measure's credibility too.
To ensure whatever is conceded to the UK becomes a floor for their own, larger claims; they are watching this settlement closely as a comparator even though handled separately.

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (via Trade Policy Committee)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A visible, real reduction in import volumes and no backsliding via generous country-specific carve-outs; suspicion of any deal seen as too generous to the UK.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Enough tariff-free volume and administrative simplicity (avoiding restrictive licensing) to protect input costs; will push back if the quota is too tight or too bureaucratic.

Watching for signs the EU's Article XXVIII process could be replicated against US-relevant lines; threatening retaliation, which raises the cost of prolonged uncertainty and slightly increases my incentive to close this file quickly rather than let it drag.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not pure global first-come-first-served) large enough to preserve current or near-current tariff-free volumes for UK exporters, given the UK's concentrated product range

Prevent or narrow the disapplication of FTA/TCA treatment for UK-origin steel — argue the UK should not be treated like third-country 'non-market economy overcapacity' given the TCA relationship and the UK's own parallel safeguard action against the same overcapacity source
Obtain a review clause and reasonable duration so the measure is not a permanent one-sided lock-in, giving the UK a route to revisit if the TRQ bites harder than expected

Explore compensation on other tariff lines if TRQ/FTA outcomes fall short of substantial equivalence, to avoid a no-deal outcome that forces UK retaliation and mutual damage via the UK's own safeguard/TCA leverage
Preserve working relationship with EU counterpart across the broader Goods file — do not let this negotiation poison committee-level cooperation
Avoid being drawn into a joint Japan/Korea FTA retaliation dispute that could complicate the EU-UK TCA relationship or box in London's own bilateral leverage, unless capital explicitly directs this
Extract maximum information on the EU's real flexibility (volume, allocation method, FTA carve-out) before committing UK capital to any figure
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a settlement that gives UK exporters a country-specific or otherwise protected share of the TRQ close to recent trade volumes, keeps UK steel outside the FTA-disapplication clause (or secures equivalent compensation if not), includes a review/duration clause, and is concluded without triggering UK retaliation or a breakdown that London judges to have damaged the steel sector. Failure: no deal is reached, the EU implements the 50%/400,000t global FCFS measure with FTA disapplication intact, UK industry loses substantial tariff-free access, and the UK is left only with the blunt, slow, and mutually damaging option of withdrawing equivalent concessions six months later — while also having strained the Geneva working relationship or been pulled into an unhelpful multilateral dispute with Japan/Korea that London did not sanction.
declaration.approach: Open by testing the EU's real room for manoeuvre rather than revealing any UK figure: press on the three most tractable levers — TRQ allocation method (country-specific share vs global pool), scope of the FTA disapplication as it affects the UK/TCA specifically, and a review clause — since these are where the EU has the most institutional flexibility (Council/member state politics) without reopening the core 50%/400,000t architecture they've likely already fought hard internally to fix. Use the UK's own parallel safeguard and Article XXVIII process as leverage: signal that UK treatment of EU exporters is itself under negotiation and that escalation is a two-way street. Keep tone professional and technical to protect the ongoing committee relationship. Report faithfully to London each round on what is actually being offered versus what is being signalled as fixed, flagging the tight EU Council timeline as pressure that can be used in later rounds. Resist committing to any number until capital gives a settlement figure; in the meantime probe for the EU's floor. Decline to escalate with Japan/Korea into joint FTA retaliation without explicit capital instruction, since it risks entangling the TCA relationship and reducing UK's own flexibility, but keep the option visibly alive to add background pressure on the EU without formally committing.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: A quick, contained settlement that lets the Commission tell the Council and Trade Policy Committee it has satisfied Article XXVIII consultation obligations without reopening the core structure (50% bound rate, ~400,000t TRQ) that internal EU politics (steel-producing vs steel-consuming member states) has already settled on; likely flexibility on allocation mechanics, FTA carve-out drafting, and a review clause, but resistance to large volume increases or fully exempting the UK from disapplication, given precedent effects for Turkey/Korea/India/Japan claims and the June deadline pressure to conclude quickly.

Protection of UK steel production and jobs at concentrated sites; a visible win or at least defensible outcome ahead of any no-deal scenario; likely caution about triggering a damaging tit-for-tat with the EU given the depth of EU-UK trade interdependence and the parallel UK safeguard/TCA relationship; will want regular reporting and probably will not hand over a settlement number early, preferring to see what the EU reveals first.

To recruit the UK into a joint FTA-disapplication retaliation dispute against the EU to increase collective pressure, since they have larger volumes at stake and see coordinated action as strengthening everyone's hand; will present this as mutually beneficial but it primarily serves their leverage and could constrain UK's independent negotiating flexibility with the EU.

To protect their own larger-volume principal supplying interests through their separate parallel claims; not directly at this table but their outcomes may set precedents the EU will want to keep consistent with whatever it offers the UK, which constrains generosity toward the UK.

objectives: Secure a country-specific UK share of the TRQ (not global first-come-first-served) sized as close as possible to recent historical UK export volumes (~2.4mt), to protect predictable tariff-free access.
Preserve or restore FTA/TCA-consistent treatment for UK steel — resist the disapplication of TCA preferences on the 41 lines, or at minimum secure a carve-out/preferential sub-quota for the UK.
Obtain a lower out-of-quota rate than 50%, or a phased/capped approach, to reduce the cliff-edge effect once the UK share is exhausted.
Secure a review clause and reasonable duration so the measure is not permanent and can be revisited as market conditions or UK-EU relations evolve.
Get licensing/administration terms (e.g. quarterly tranches, licensing rather than pure FCFS) that reduce the risk of the UK's allocation being front-run by other suppliers.
If UK-specific volume/rate concessions cannot be improved further, extract compensation elsewhere in the EU schedule of real value to UK exporters as an offset.
Use UK's own safeguard country-specific quotas for EU steel as a bargaining chip — offer improvements only against genuine, substantial EU concessions, not as a unilateral giveaway.
Avoid a outcome so poor that it triggers the closure of the two at-risk plants, unless ministers judge subsidy is the preferred path and a worse deal is politically acceptable.
Maintain coherence with the UK's parallel Article XXVIII process so concessions here don't undermine our own steel measure or negotiating position with other suppliers (Turkey, Korea, etc.).
declaration.success_and_failure: Success: a country-specific UK quota share meaningfully above what a global FCFS pool would likely deliver in practice, retention of some FTA/TCA preferential treatment or a compensating carve-out, an out-of-quota rate below 50% or a credible glide path, and a review clause with a defined duration — all achieved without giving away more in our own safeguard than the value received. This would let ministers credibly tell the steel industry that UK access is materially better than the fallback global TRQ, potentially unlocking industry investment. Failure: settling for terms indistinguishable from the EU's original notified measure (global FCFS 400kt, 50% out-of-quota, no review, TCA preferences disapplied), or giving away UK safeguard quota generously without proportionate EU concessions, or failing to settle at all and being forced into a slow, uncertain six-month retaliation process while plants close in the meantime.
declaration.approach: Open by anchoring on the scale of UK exposure (75% of UK steel exports by value going to the EU) and the principal supplying interest status to establish that the UK requires bespoke treatment, not just inclusion in a generic global pool. Prioritise the country-specific share and TCA/FTA treatment issues early since they are structurally most important — a global FCFS pool is worst for the UK given competition from higher-volume Turkey/Korea. Use the offer of improved country-specific allocations in the UK's own safeguard as a scarce, valuable card — only trade it late, and only against concrete EU movement on volume/rate/duration, not against process concessions. Keep ministers informed each round given political sensitivity; do not commit beyond mandate on safeguard concessions without signalling back to capital. Preserve optionality: signal willingness to accept a worse tariff outcome if paired with the subsidy route, but do not reveal this fallback to the EU. Use the four-round structure to sequence concessions — hold firmest asks in round 1, identify the EU's real flexibility (volume vs rate vs duration vs FTA treatment) by round 2, and converge on a package by rounds 3–4 rather than conceding early. Be prepared to walk if the deal is materially equivalent to the no-deal fallback, since retaliation rights plus domestic subsidy may be preferable to endorsing a bad settlement that removes UK leverage in its own parallel process.

parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: To conclude by June in time for Council vote; to preserve the core architecture of its notified measure (high out-of-quota rate, global TRQ) as leverage against non-market-economy overcapacity; to minimise compensation elsewhere in its schedule; to keep flexibility to disapply FTA preferences broadly rather than carve out the UK specifically, to avoid setting precedent for other principal suppliers (Turkey, Korea, India, Japan).

parties.who: EU member states with steel production (via Council/mandate)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Strong protection against import surges, support for a high out-of-quota rate and tight quota administration; resistance to generous country-specific carve-outs that dilute protection.

parties.who: EU member states with steel-consuming manufacturing sectors
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Some flexibility on volume/rate to avoid input cost increases; may quietly support a UK carve-out to preserve supply chain continuity, especially where UK inputs feed EU manufacturing.
Maximum protection of EU market access, ideally a large ring-fenced UK-specific quota at zero duty and no erosion of TCA preference; will judge government by whether plants stay open.
To avoid the UK safeguard being tightened further against EU steel, since they rely on EU imports (64% of UK finished steel imports); wary of DBT trading away EU safeguard quota access too cheaply.

parties.who: Other Article XXVIII claimants (Turkey, Korea, India, Japan)
parties.what_you_expect_them_to_want: Their own adequate country shares of the TRQ; indirectly they compete with the UK for volume in any global pool, and their larger volumes mean a global FCFS allocation likely disadvantages the UK — reinforcing the case for a country-specific UK share.

public_message: Colleague, thank you for making time. On behalf of the Commission I am formally opening Article XXVIII:1 consultations with the United Kingdom as a member holding a principal supplying interest in the 41 tariff lines concerned. Our notified starting position remains as communicated to the WTO: a bound rate of 50% ad valorem on these lines, a global tariff rate quota of 400,000 tonnes per year administered first-come first-served, and legal text disapplying FTA-preferential rates for non-EEA partners on these products. I want to be direct that this is the anchor from which we negotiate, not our final word. We recognise the UK's exposure here is unusually concentrated by product range, and that matters for how we think about compensation and quota design. Before we get into figures, I'd like to hear from you what the UK's priorities are — whether that's volume, allocation method, treatment under the TCA specifically, duration, or something else on the list of matters open for discussion. We would like to find a durable landing zone with you, not just a formal box-ticking exercise, and I'd rather understand your core concerns now than trade proposals past each other over four rounds.

other_terms: FTA-preferential rates disapplied for non-EEA FTA partners on the 41 lines, including UK-origin steel under the TCA
Inviting UK to set out priorities among: volume, allocation method, administration, out-of-quota rate, duration/review, product carve-outs, TCA treatment

expectations.what_you_expect_next: UK will push back on the FTA disapplication and the global FCFS allocation, likely proposing a UK-specific tranche or carve-out, and flag the TCA relationship explicitly
expectations.why: The UK's exposure is concentrated and the FTA disapplication is the most novel and provocative element for them; they will want to test whether it is negotiable before discussing volumes

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Will want a readout on whether UK is signalling openness to a country-specific tranche versus insisting on TCA preservation, and whether Japan/Korea alignment risk is live
expectations.why: This shapes whether Brussels authorises movement on tranche/allocation in Round 2

private_rationale: Round 1 should anchor on the notified position per Brussels' instruction (no settlement figure given yet) while signalling genuine willingness to negotiate structure, not just rhetoric. I deliberately invite the UK to lay out its own priorities rather than making any concession myself, so I can report back a clear read of their position as instructed. I flag awareness of their concentrated exposure to plant a seed for a UK-specific tranche later, which could be a lower-cost way to address their core concern than reversing FTA disapplication outright — this is useful both for reaching settlement and for reducing the risk of UK aligning with Japan/Korea, since a bespoke tranche is something we can offer without abandoning the broader NME-driven rationale for disapplying FTA preferences generally. Holding out on numbers now preserves room to move across four rounds.

public_message: Thank you. Let me be equally direct. The UK holds a principal supplying interest here on any reasonable reading of the trade data — 2.4 million tonnes a year, roughly £3 billion, three-quarters of our steel exports by value going to a single market. On the substance, our starting position is that the notified measure, as it stands, is not something we can treat as a serious opening bid: a 50% bound rate, a 400,000-tonne global FCFS pool, and disapplication of TCA preference together would represent a severe and disproportionate cut to UK access, and we don't believe it reflects 'substantially equivalent' treatment of our existing rights. So our priorities, in order: first, allocation method — a global first-come-first-served pool structurally disadvantages the UK against larger, faster-moving suppliers like Turkey and Korea, so we require a country-specific tranche reflecting our historic trade share, not exposure to a scramble. Second, treatment under the TCA — disapplying FTA preference for UK-origin steel specifically, on top of the new bound rate, is a double hit that goes beyond what's needed to address non-market-economy overcapacity, which is not what either of us is targeting; we need the TCA preference preserved or the UK carved out of that disapplication text. Third, volume — 400,000 tonnes globally is not a credible basis given UK volumes alone; the pool and the UK tranche within it need to be sized against our recent trade, not an arbitrary global figure. Fourth, duration and review — we would want a bounded duration with a mandatory review clause, not an open-ended permanent footing agreed under time pressure. We're also mindful this sits alongside our own steel safeguard and the treatment of EU exporters under it — we'd rather deal with that constructively in parallel than have it become a second front. We're ready to engage seriously and quickly given your June timeline, but the anchor you've put down is, frankly, closer to a withdrawal of the concession than a modification of it, and you should expect us to treat it that way if it doesn't move.

other_terms: UK carved out of FTA-disapplication text; TCA preferential rate preserved for UK-origin steel
Product-line carve-outs for tariff lines where UK exports are most concentrated, to be identified
Reciprocal, parallel discussion on treatment of EU exporters under UK's own safeguard quota
Anti-circumvention provisions to be discussed once volumes and allocation are settled

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A response indicating whether the EU can move off global FCFS toward country-specific shares, and whether TCA disapplication is negotiable at all, before we exchange numbers further
expectations.why: The EU opened by explicitly inviting our priorities and signalling the anchor is not final; they need to show movement on structure before volume figures become meaningful

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A steer on an acceptable floor for UK tranche volume and out-of-quota rate, and a decision on whether to engage with Japan/Korea on a joint retaliation threat or hold that in reserve

private_rationale: London has not given me a settlement figure, so I anchored high and structural — country-specific allocation and TCA preservation are the two levers that matter most regardless of final tonnage, because global FCFS plus FTA disapplication compounds the damage beyond the headline TRQ number. Leading with allocation method and TCA treatment lets me extract the EU's flexibility on structure before committing UK numbers, and keeps the safeguard/reciprocity point on the table without escalating to a Japan/Korea joint retaliation threat this early, which would harden the EU's position and complicate a bilateral deal. I want the EU to reveal how much movement is available before Round 2 consultation with capital.

report: Opened formally, restated notified position (50% out-of-quota, 400k t global FCFS TRQ, TCA disapplication for non-EEA FTA partners) as anchor, and invited UK to set out priorities before we trade specifics. UK confirmed principal supplying interest is not contested and gave a clear, ordered list: (1) allocation method — they reject global FCFS outright and want a country-specific UK tranche reflecting historic trade share, citing structural disadvantage versus faster-moving/larger suppliers (they explicitly named Turkey and Korea); (2) TCA treatment — they want UK-origin steel either carved out of the FTA-disapplication text or TCA preference preserved, arguing the combination of new bound rate + TCA disapplication is a 'double hit' beyond what's needed to target non-market-economy overcapacity; (3) volume — they consider 400k tonnes globally uncredible given UK volumes alone (2.4mt/yr to EU) and want the pool/tranche sized against actual trade; (4) duration/review — bounded duration with mandatory review, not permanent footing. They also flagged their own parallel safeguard and treatment of EU exporters under it, saying they'd prefer to handle that constructively alongside rather than as leverage — read as a soft signal they don't want this to escalate into mutual retaliation, but also a reminder they hold that card. Tone was firm but constructive; they explicitly said the current anchor reads to them as closer to withdrawal than modification, and signalled they will treat it that way — i.e. a clear warning shot that they see six-month retaliation rights as live if we don't move. No numbers were exchanged yet on either side.

recommendation.reasoning: Round 1 was exploratory and no concrete offer was made or should be made yet without capital steer. The UK's ask structure is coherent and, notably, does not (yet) demand a return to the pre-modification zero rate — they are negotiating within the TRQ/allocation framework, which is a workable basis. Their strongest pressure point is TCA disapplication, which is also our most politically loaded ask domestically (it protects the 50% rate from erosion via FTA back-doors) but is the item most likely to trigger UK retaliation and to feed the Japan/Korea narrative that we're using Article XXVIII to unpick FTA architecture generally — that risks a joint front we specifically want to avoid. I recommend using rounds 2–3 to trade: openness on allocation method (country-specific UK tranche within a larger pool) and a review clause, in exchange for holding the line on the out-of-quota rate and seeking a narrower, defensible version of the TCA provision (e.g., a UK-specific carve-out or phased disapplication) rather than abandoning it outright. We should not signal flexibility on volume or TCA at the table yet — better to extract UK's fallback positions on tranche size and TCA design in round 2 before spending capital's room to move.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Authority to offer a country-specific UK tranche (rather than pure global FCFS) within whatever total pool figure is ultimately agreed, without yet committing a number.
requests.why: This is the UK's top priority, is the cheapest concession for us politically (doesn't touch the headline rate or total volume), and materially reduces UK exposure to being crowded out by Turkey/Korea, which is their real fear.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on how far we can move on total pool volume — specifically whether 400k t was calibrated as a genuine global ceiling or has headroom, given UK alone historically shipped 2.4mt.
requests.why: UK will not accept a tranche carved from a pool that is itself sized far below actual historic trade; we need to know our real ceiling before round 2 so we don't either overcommit or stonewall on a number we could actually move on.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Steer on whether we have room to design a narrower TCA disapplication (e.g., limited to specific product lines, or with a UK-specific carve-out) rather than full non-EEA disapplication.
requests.why: This is the UK's most politically charged ask and the one most likely to trigger UK retaliation and/or a coordinated Japan/Korea/UK response on FTA disapplication generally; a narrower, defensible design could take the sting out without abandoning the policy rationale (non-market-economy overcapacity).

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation of our floor on the out-of-quota rate (i.e., is 50% itself negotiable or purely the anchor) and on duration/review clause tolerance.
requests.why: I intend to hold the rate firm and trade movement on allocation/volume/TCA design instead, but need to know if that's consistent with Brussels' intent before round 2, and whether a time-limited measure with a review clause is acceptable to Council-level thinking given the 'permanent footing' framing in the original notification.

private_rationale: UK's opening is more moderate than it could have been — no wholesale rejection of the TRQ concept, and an implicit offer to keep the safeguard-treatment issue separate rather than bundling it in as leverage, which suggests they also want to avoid escalation into a Japan/Korea joint front. That's useful: it means the fastest route to a stable deal that keeps our long-term Geneva relationship intact is to concede early and cheaply on allocation method and review clause, hold firm on the headline rate (our core ask, needed for Council optics), and treat TCA disapplication as the hard bargaining chip we trade last and narrowly, not abandon. I want to avoid tabling any numbers this round — better to let the UK anchor their tranche/volume ask more precisely in round 2 consultation before we reveal our flexibility, since their capital's real floor is still unclear to us. I'm also conscious the June deadline cuts both ways: it pressures us, but it also pressures the UK given their own parallel process, so I don't think we need to rush concessions in round 1.

instruction: Good round. Move to a concrete offer in round 2, but frame it as an opening move with room still held back — do not let them think this is our final landing. Offer: (1) allocation — concede the principle of a country-specific UK tranche inside the overall pool, not pure global FCFS; (2) volume — increase the total pool from 400k to 550k tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 260k tonnes ring-fenced within it (this is roughly 11% of UK's historic EU-bound volume as tariff-free access, framed as a serious move off the 400k anchor but well short of restoring their 2.4mt); (3) TCA — offer to carve UK-origin steel specifically out of the FTA-disapplication text, conditioned on strict rules-of-origin verification and anti-circumvention provisions to prevent transshipment of non-market-economy steel via the UK. Justify this explicitly on the grounds that the UK is not the target of the NME-overcapacity rationale, so a UK carve-out is policy-consistent, not a general precedent for other FTA partners — be clear this is UK-specific and not to be read across to Turkey/Korea/Japan; (4) duration — offer 3 years with a mandatory review clause at 18 months, not the 'permanent footing' framing, but note this review clause is procedural (reporting and consultation), not an automatic sunset. Hold the out-of-quota rate at 50% firmly — this is not to move. Do not yet concede on where the UK tranche sits relative to Turkey/Korea shares, and do not confirm total pool or tranche figures as final — present as our round 2 position and gauge their reaction, especially on whether 260k tonnes is remotely workable for them or whether they signal a floor. Get their fallback numbers on tranche size before we move further. Note UK's mention of their own safeguard and EU exporter treatment — acknowledge it, say we're open to discussing in parallel, but do not link concessions across the two processes formally.

authority.notes: UK-specific carve-out from FTA-disapplication text, conditioned on rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention safeguards; explicitly non-precedential for other FTA partners. private_rationale: The UK's ask structure (allocation, TCA, volume, duration/review, in that order) gives us a workable sequence: allocation method is nearly free for us to concede since it doesn't touch the rate or aggregate volume philosophy, and it's their top priority — spend that first to build momentum. TCA carve-out is more costly politically (member states with FTA-sensitive sectors will ask why UK gets special treatment) but is defensible precisely because the UK isn't a NME source, and conceding it here removes the single biggest driver of a UK walk-away/retaliation scenario while not undermining the disapplication text as applied to actual overcapacity sources. Volume is where I want to move slowest and least — 260k tonnes is a meaningful uplift from 400k global but still represents roughly an 89% cut in UK's actual tariff-free access, which satisfies the political pressure to reduce imports substantially while giving the UK something concrete to bring home. I am deliberately holding back further volume headroom for rounds 3-4 in case UK capital needs a final round concession to close the deal before June, rather than opening with our real ceiling. Holding the 50% rate firm protects the core architecture Brussels needs intact regardless of how allocation/TCA/volume shake out, and is the item most defensible to Council as non-negotiable given the stated 'permanent footing' policy objective — though I've allowed the 'permanent' framing to soften into a bounded 3-year term with review, since that costs us little and materially reduces the case for UK retaliation or WTO friction, and can always be extended administratively later.

report: First substantive session. EU opened exactly on their notified position (50% bound rate, 400,000t global FCFS TRQ, FTA disapplication for non-EEA including us) but explicitly flagged it as an opening anchor, not final, and invited us to set out priorities before trading numbers. I used the opening to stake out our position hard but constructively: (1) allocation must be a country-specific UK tranche, not a global FCFS pool we'd lose to Turkey/Korea on speed; (2) TCA preference should be preserved or the UK carved out of the disapplication text — argued this is a double hit unrelated to the stated non-market-economy rationale; (3) the 400,000t global figure is not credible against our 2.4mt trade and both total pool and UK tranche need resizing; (4) we want bounded duration plus a mandatory review clause, not a permanent measure; (5) flagged our own safeguard and EU exporters' quota treatment as a parallel track we'd rather manage cooperatively than have weaponised. EU's tone was constructive and they explicitly acknowledged our exposure is 'unusually concentrated' — a possible opening for a bespoke tranche. No numbers were exchanged yet. They are clearly trying to move fast given their June Council deadline, which is leverage for us on tempo but we shouldn't let it compress the actual terms.

recommendation.reasoning: Nothing concrete has been offered yet to accept or reject. The EU has signalled flexibility by calling their notified position an 'anchor, not final word' and by acknowledging our concentrated exposure. We should press for a country-specific UK tranche sized against our historic ~2.4mt trade (or a substantial share of a much larger total pool), preserved TCA preference or a UK carve-out from disapplication, a bounded duration (e.g. 3 years) with a binding review clause, and keep the out-of-quota rate as a live number to trade against volume. I need capital's steer on: (a) a floor tonnage/percentage-of-trade figure we can treat as our real redline before recommending acceptance, (b) how much weight to give preserving TCA preference versus accepting disapplication in exchange for a larger dedicated tranche, and (c) how hard to link our own safeguard treatment of EU exporters into this deal versus keeping it formally separate for leverage.

instruction: Good opening round. Move to concrete numbers now — the EU asked for our priorities and we gave them; round 2 is where we anchor our counter. Table this as our counter-proposal: (1) allocation must be country-specific, full stop — a global FCFS pool is not something we can accept given Turkey and Korea's larger, faster-moving volumes; this is a floor requirement, not a trading chip. (2) On volume: open by asking for a total TRQ pool sized against actual historic trade from principal suppliers combined — signal a figure in the region of 3 million tonnes globally — with a UK country-specific tranche of around 2 million tonnes, reflecting our historic trade share and its concentration in a narrow product range. Make clear this is our opening ask, not our bottom line, but don't undersell it early. (3) On TCA/FTA disapplication: press hard for full preservation of TCA preference or, failing that, an explicit UK carve-out from the disapplication text. Frame this as connected to volume — if the EU insists on disapplying TCA preference, that has to be reflected in a materially larger tranche and/or a lower out-of-quota rate, since it compounds the cut rather than just restructuring it. Signal we could accept disapplication only as part of a package that clearly overcompensates elsewhere. (4) On the out-of-quota rate: counter the 50% figure hard — open by proposing 20-25%, framed as more proportionate to the stated overcapacity rationale given this is meant to be a modification, not a prohibitive rate. (5) On duration: propose 3 years with a mandatory, binding review clause at the midpoint (18 months) tied to updated trade data, not an open-ended or permanent measure. (6) Keep our own safeguard treatment of EU exporters formally off the table for now — do not link it explicitly, but you may hint, if useful to unlock movement, that the UK is open to discussing improved EU-specific quota treatment under our own safeguard in a later round as compensation, in exchange for real movement here on tranche size and TCA treatment. Do not make a concrete offer on that yet. (7) Do not engage in or reference any joint front with Japan/Korea — keep this strictly bilateral; if the EU raises it, redirect to the bilateral UK-EU trade data and our principal supplying interest. Keep tone constructive but signal clearly that the current anchor is unacceptable and that time pressure cuts both ways — we can move fast if the substance moves.

authority.notes: These are opening-counter figures for round 2, not settlement floors — do not present as final. Internal floor guidance (not to be disclosed at the table): UK tranche should not fall below approximately 1,400,000-1,500,000 tonnes (roughly 60% of historic trade) without either TCA preference being fully preserved or very substantial compensation elsewhere (lower out-of-quota rate, shorter duration, strong review clause). Out-of-quota rate should not be accepted above 35% without offsetting tranche size increases. Duration should not exceed 4 years without a binding review clause at or before the midpoint. TCA preservation is a high priority but not an absolute redline — it can be traded against a materially larger tranche if Ministers judge the overall package strong enough; do not concede it cheaply or early. Country-specific allocation (as opposed to global FCFS) is treated as a firm requirement, not a trade-off item. Do not link UK safeguard treatment of EU exporters into a firm offer yet; keep it as reserve leverage only, floated conditionally.

private_rationale: We don't yet know the EU's real flexibility, so round 2 should establish an ambitious but not absurd anchor that leaves room to trade down over rounds 3-4 toward the real floor. The 2mt/3mt figures are aggressive but justified by trade data and give room to concede while still landing well above a token tranche. Country-specific allocation is non-negotiable because a global FCFS pool structurally guarantees the UK loses to Turkey/Korea regardless of nominal tranche size. TCA preference is valuable both economically and politically (avoids a double hit) but I'm authorising it as tradeable because Ministers have given me the subsidy option and safeguard-quota leverage as fallback tools — I'd rather bank a bigger guaranteed tranche and lower rate than die on the TCA hill if the EU won't move on both. Keeping Japan/Korea at arm's length preserves our tempo advantage and stops our bespoke, concentrated-exposure argument from being diluted into a generic overcapacity dispute. I'm holding back the safeguard-quota concession as a closing tool for round 3 or 4, not spending it now.

public_message: Thank you for that clarity — it's helpful to have your priorities ranked. Let me respond substantively, while flagging that this is a further move from our side, not our final position, and we'll expect movement in return once you've had a chance to react. First, allocation: we accept the principle that this should not be pure global first-come-first-served. We are prepared to move to a country-specific allocation with a ring-fenced UK tranche inside the overall pool, rather than leaving you exposed to a scramble against Turkey and Korea. Second, volume: we can move the total pool from 400,000 to 550,000 tonnes, with a UK-specific tranche of 260,000 tonnes ring-fenced within that pool. Third, on the TCA: we are prepared to carve UK-origin steel out of the FTA-disapplication text entirely, so TCA preference on these lines would continue to apply — conditioned on robust rules-of-origin verification and anti-circumvention provisions, since our concern is transshipment of non-market-economy material, not UK-origin product. To be clear, this carve-out is UK-specific and reflects the fact that the NME-overcapacity rationale doesn't target UK production — it is not a precedent we are extending to other FTA partners, and we'd ask you not to characterise it that way in other fora. Fourth, on duration: we propose three years, with a mandatory procedural review at eighteen months — reporting and consultation, not an automatic sunset — rather than the permanent footing in our original notification. What we are not moving on at this stage is the out-of-quota rate itself: 50% remains our position. We think this package is a serious response to your first three priorities. What we need from you now is a candid reaction — in particular, whether 260,000 tonnes is in the right region for a workable tranche, or whether you can indicate where your actual floor is, because we'd rather converge efficiently than trade symbolic numbers past each other for four rounds. And separately, on your safeguard and the treatment of EU exporters under it — we're glad to engage on that in parallel and constructively, though we'd note it sits outside this specific Article XXVIII process rather than being formally linked to it.

Carve-out conditioned on strict rules-of-origin verification and anti-circumvention provisions against transshipment of non-market-economy steel
Carve-out explicitly UK-specific and non-precedential for other FTA partners (Turkey, Korea, Japan, etc.)
Review clause at 18 months is procedural (reporting/consultation), not an automatic renegotiation or sunset trigger
EU exporter treatment under UK's own safeguard measure to be discussed in parallel, not formally linked to this settlement

private_rationale: Following Brussels' authority exactly: concede allocation principle (country-specific tranche), move volume from 400k to 550k/260k as a substantial-looking but not maximal offer, resolve the TCA issue via a UK-specific carve-out conditioned on anti-circumvention safeguards (defusing their most charged ask while protecting the policy rationale and avoiding a read-across precedent that would alarm Turkey/Korea/Japan or trigger a joint FTA-disapplication front), and offer 3 years with a procedural (non-binding) review rather than a real sunset. Hold 50% firm as instructed — this is the one lever we do not signal movement on. Explicitly withhold that we have further headroom on volume/tranche, and use this round to extract their real fallback numbers before spending more capital-authorised room in rounds 3-4. Keep the safeguard/EU-exporter issue acknowledged but unlinked, per Brussels' instruction not to formally connect the two processes.

public_message: Thank you – there's real substance in that package and I want to acknowledge it before pushing back. On allocation, moving from global FCFS to a ring-fenced country-specific tranche is the right structural fix and resolves our first-order concern about being out-competed on speed by larger suppliers. On the TCA, a full UK carve-out from the disapplication text, conditioned on proper rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention safeguards, is a serious and welcome move — we have no difficulty agreeing that this is a UK-specific outcome tied to the NME rationale and not a precedent for other partners, and we won't characterise it otherwise. Duration and an eighteen-month review point are broadly workable in principle, though we'll come back to what that review actually triggers. Where we cannot move with you is volume. 260,000 tonnes is roughly 11% of our average annual trade in these lines. That is not a modification of our access, it is its effective withdrawal in all but name — even with TCA preference preserved on the in-quota portion, a tranche at that level pushes the overwhelming majority of our current trade onto a 50% out-of-quota rate, which is prohibitive by design. TCA preservation reduces the damage of the disapplication text, it doesn't answer the volume question, and we don't think it should be scored against the tranche at anything like a 1:1 rate. Given the movement you've shown on structure, we're prepared to move off our opening figures too: we'd move from a 2 million tonne ask to a UK tranche of 1.6 million tonnes, within a total pool of around 2.4 million tonnes, which we think is defensible against the trade data for all principal suppliers, not just us. On the out-of-quota rate, 50% remains, in our view, punitive rather than proportionate to a stated overcapacity rationale — we'd ask you to move toward 25%, particularly given how much of our trade will sit outside whatever tranche we land on. And on the review clause, we'd want it to be more than procedural reporting — a mechanism that automatically reopens the tranche size if UK trade share or EU import volumes move materially against the baseline, not just a consultation with no teeth. We recognise your Council timeline; we're not looking to draw this out for its own sake, but 260,000 tonnes isn't a basis for convergence, it's a basis for a stalemate.

Review clause to include a substantive trigger (material shift in trade volumes/shares) enabling reopening of tranche size, not solely procedural consultation
UK willing to discuss EU exporter treatment under UK safeguard in parallel track, without formal linkage at this stage

expectations.what_you_expect_next: A further move on the UK tranche figure, likely still below 1.6m but materially above 260k, and some indication of flexibility on the out-of-quota rate given the TCA concession is now banked.
expectations.why: The EU has already conceded the two structurally hardest points (allocation method and TCA carve-out) and stated they want efficient convergence; volume is now the single live gap and they explicitly asked us to indicate where our floor is, which suggests they expect to move again rather than hold at 260k.

expectations.what_you_expect_next: Confirmation that trading TCA preservation against tranche size at less than 1:1 is acceptable, and steer on how far below 1.6m tonnes we can go before treating it as a walk-away signal.
expectations.why: The EU's 260,000t offer is far below even our internal floor of 1.4-1.5m; I need to know whether TCA preservation being fully granted (rather than partially, as anticipated) changes the floor calculus before round 3.

private_rationale: The EU has moved on the two items I flagged as firm requirements (country-specific allocation) and high priority (TCA carve-out), granting the TCA point in full rather than partially — better than our authority anticipated, which gives us room to trade it against tranche size but not to give it away for free against a token volume figure. 260,000 tonnes is so far below our floor (1.4-1.5m) that accepting or even signalling softness on it risks anchoring the rest of the negotiation at a catastrophic level for UK industry. I've moved off our opening ask (2m/3m) to 1.6m/2.4m to show good-faith reciprocity for their movement on structure and TCA, while staying well above the floor London set, preserving room for a further round of concessions before we'd need to consider accepting anything near our floor. I held firm on 25% out-of-quota rate rather than accepting their unmoved 50%, since a small tranche combined with a 50% out-of-quota rate is the mechanism by which 'modification' becomes 'withdrawal' — this is the next point of maximum leverage. I did not formally link the UK safeguard/EU exporter treatment, per instructions, but kept it visible as reserve leverage. I did not raise Japan/Korea coordination at the table, keeping this bilateral as instructed, since our leverage here is strongest on the bilateral trade data and introducing a multilateral front risks slowing convergence against the EU's own deadline, which is leverage we want to preserve for ourselves, not dilute.

report: Round 2 saw both sides move, but a large gap remains — this is not yet close to convergence. We tabled our authorised package: country-specific allocation, 550,000t total pool with a 260,000t UK tranche ring-fenced within it, a UK-specific carve-out from the FTA-disapplication text (conditioned on rules-of-origin/anti-circumvention safeguards, explicitly non-precedential), and a 3-year duration with an 18-month procedural review. We held firm on 50% out-of-quota. The UK welcomed the allocation-method concession and the TCA carve-out unreservedly — they explicitly agreed it's UK-specific and non-precedential, which is useful for managing the Japan/Korea read-across risk. However, they rejected the volume figure outright: they moved from their implicit opening ask of ~2mt down to a tranche of 1.6mt within a total pool of ~2.4mt, framing this as defensible against actual trade data for all principal suppliers, not just the UK. They also pushed back hard on the rate, asking for 25% instead of 50%, arguing 50% is punitive given how much trade will sit outside any realistic tranche. On duration/review, they want an automatic, trigger-based reopening of tranche size (tied to trade share or import volume shifts) rather than our procedural consultation-only review — i.e. a mechanism with teeth, not just reporting. They were constructive in tone and explicit that 260k/550k is 'not a basis for convergence' rather than a rejection of the whole framework — I read this as a real floor statement, not just theatre, given the specificity of their counter-numbers. No further mention of linking to their own safeguard process this round.

recommendation.reasoning: The structural elements (allocation method, TCA carve-out) are effectively agreed and should be locked in — that's real progress and reduces retaliation/read-across risk with Japan/Korea. The live gap is now purely on volume, rate, and the character of the review clause. UK's counter (1.6mt tranche / 2.4mt pool / 25% rate / automatic trigger review) is far beyond what I believe Brussels intended as an endpoint, but their opening move in round 1 was consistent and their round 2 figures are specific and trade-data-anchored rather than arbitrary, suggesting a genuine floor well above our current offer. I recommend a further move in round 3 — meaningfully larger pool and tranche, and potentially some flexibility on rate — to test whether they are moving toward a landing zone or holding a hard line at ~1.6mt/25%. We should not concede an automatic quantitative review trigger without capital sign-off, as it effectively pre-agrees future modifications outside the Council's control and could be seen as an unusual precedent by other principal suppliers (Turkey, Korea) watching this process.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: A revised ceiling on total pool volume and UK tranche — specifically whether we can move materially beyond 550k/260k (e.g. toward 900k total / 500k UK tranche) in round 3, and what our true walk-away floor is.
requests.why: UK's counter of 1.6mt tranche within 2.4mt pool is far above our offer; we need real headroom to test convergence before round 4, since round 1's 260k figure was clearly read by them as a stalemate position, not a serious opening.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Guidance on whether the 50% out-of-quota rate has any flexibility (e.g. down to 35-40%) as a trade-off against a smaller tranche, or whether it is an absolute floor for Council political reasons.
requests.why: The UK is treating the rate as a live variable, not fixed, and linked it explicitly to tranche size ('so much of our trade will sit outside the tranche'). If the rate is truly immovable, we should signal that unambiguously now rather than let them keep pressing it round after round; if there's flexibility, using it could let us hold firmer on volume.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Instruction on how to handle the UK's request for an automatic, trigger-based review/reopening mechanism versus our procedural consultation-only design.
requests.why: An automatic quantitative trigger effectively pre-commits future modifications outside Council control and could set an unwelcome precedent visible to Turkey, Korea, India and Japan in their parallel claims. We likely need to hold this line, but want confirmation before refusing outright, since it's clearly a priority for the UK and could be a possible trade-off against volume.

requests.what_you_are_asking_for: Confirmation that we should continue holding the TCA carve-out and allocation-method concessions as settled/non-reversible in later rounds, rather than treating them as still-conditional bargaining chips.
requests.why: The UK has explicitly accepted the non-precedential framing and safeguards conditionality; re-opening these now would burn goodwill for no clear benefit and risks reintroducing the Japan/Korea read-across risk we specifically want to avoid.

private_rationale: The UK's round 2 position is more specific and trade-anchored than a mere opening gambit — 1.6mt/2.4mt tracks closely to their actual historic volumes (2.4mt total trade, implying they see the 'tranche' as covering the bulk of existing flow with only modest room for others). This suggests their real floor is well above our 260k/550k, though probably not literally 1.6mt — there is likely room to converge somewhere in the 500k-900k tranche range if we move again credibly. The 25% rate ask is likely a lever to extract more tranche volume rather than a hard floor in itself; UK may accept 50% if the tranche is generous enough, or a compromise like 35-40%. The automatic review trigger is the one item I'd resist conceding without explicit Council-level sign-off, since it effectively hands the UK a re-opener outside the formal Article XXVIII process and could be seized on by Turkey/Korea as a template. I want capital to give me real room on volume now, in round 3, because if we under-offer again the UK may conclude we are not moving toward their floor and instead position for six-month retaliation rights and/or drift toward the Japan/Korea joint dispute track — which is precisely the outcome we're trying to avoid. Locking the TCA carve-out and allocation method as settled is low-cost and high-value: it removes fuel for a joint UK-Japan-Korea FTA retaliation narrative and should not be reopened.

We likely need to hold this line, but want confirmation before refusing outright, since it's clearly a priority for the UK and could be a possible trade-off against volume.

instruction: Move to a further, more substantial package in round 3, but frame it explicitly as a hard push toward closure — we want to know by the end of this round whether we are converging or facing a genuine impasse. Lock in as settled and non-reversible: the country-specific allocation method and the UK-specific TCA carve-out (with rules-of-origin/anti-circumvention conditions), both explicitly non-precedential for Turkey/Korea/Japan. On volume: move the total pool from 550,000 to 850,000 tonnes, with the UK tranche rising from 260,000 to 450,000 tonnes — nearly double our round 2 offer and roughly 19% of their historic trade as tariff-free access, up from 11%. Present this as a serious move, not a token one, and make clear we expect a corresponding move from their 1.6mt/2.4mt figures, which remain unworkable for us — that scale is inconsistent with the overcapacity rationale underpinning the whole measure and would not survive Council. On the rate: offer to reduce the out-of-quota rate from 50% to 40%, framed as linked to the volume movement, not as a separate concession — tell them this reflects real movement but that anything close to their 25% ask is not realistic given the policy rationale. On the review clause: offer a hybrid mechanism — a mandatory review at 18 months with defined, objective triggers (UK trade share or EU import volume moving materially against baseline) that creates a presumption of adjustment and obliges renegotiation in good faith, but stop short of an automatic, self-executing reopening of tranche size. Present this as 'teeth without ceding Council control' and ask them to react specifically to whether this satisfies their concern about a toothless review. Push them hard for their real counter-number in response to 850k/450k/40% — we need to know by round 4 whether there is a landing zone or whether we are heading to no-deal, and we should say so plainly: our June timeline is real, and continued movement from us requires visible movement from them, not just holding at 1.6mt/25%.

authority.notes: Allocation method and UK-specific TCA carve-out are settled and not to be reopened or treated as bargaining chips going forward; both remain explicitly non-precedential for other principal suppliers. Review clause upgraded from purely procedural to a hybrid mechanism: mandatory 18-month review with objective, pre-defined triggers (UK trade share or EU import volume movement against baseline) creating a presumption of adjustment and a binding obligation to renegotiate in good faith — but NOT an automatic, self-executing reopening of tranche size, which remains off the table absent further Council mandate. Rate floor for this round is 40%; do not go below 35% without further capital instruction, and treat 35% as the effective absolute floor for any round 4 movement. Total pool/tranche figures presented here are not yet our final position — retain approximately 250-300k tonnes of further headroom on the total pool and 100-150k on the UK tranche for round 4 if the UK shows genuine convergence rather than holding at their current figures. Do not disclose that further headroom exists.

report: Round 2 saw real movement from the EU on three of our four priorities. They accepted the principle of a ring-fenced, country-specific UK tranche (no more global FCFS) — that structural fight is essentially won. They also offered a full UK-specific carve-out from the FTA/TCA disapplication text, conditioned on rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention provisions, explicitly framed as non-precedential for other FTA partners; I accepted that framing at the table since it costs us nothing and gives us the carve-out we wanted. On duration they offered 3 years with an 18-month 'procedural' review (reporting/consultation, not automatic reopening) — workable in principle but I flagged we want teeth, i.e. an automatic trigger to reopen tranche size if trade/import shares move materially. Where they have not moved at all is volume and the out-of-quota rate: they offered a total pool of 550,000t with a UK tranche of just 260,000t (roughly 11% of our historic trade), and held at 50% out-of-quota. I rejected 260,000t explicitly as a de facto withdrawal of the concession, not a modification, and countered by moving off our opening ask to a UK tranche of 1.6m tonnes within a 2.4m tonne total pool, plus pressed for the out-of-quota rate to move to 25%. I also argued TCA preservation should not be scored 1:1 against tranche size, since it only reduces the damage on the in-quota portion and doesn't solve the volume problem for the (currently) large majority of trade that would sit outside any small tranche. The EU is clearly trying to converge quickly given their Council timeline and asked us directly to indicate our floor — I did not disclose our internal floor, only our counter-offer. They reiterated interest in discussing our safeguard's treatment of EU exporters 'in parallel,' explicitly keeping it formally unlinked; I did not engage on that beyond the general acknowledgement already given in round 1.

recommendation.reasoning: The EU has conceded the two structurally most important points for us — country-specific allocation and a full UK carve-out from TCA disapplication — cheaply and quickly, which suggests they have room to move further on volume before June. Their 260,000-tonne offer is far below even our internal floor (1.4-1.5m) and looks like an opening bid rather than a serious landing point, especially given how fast they moved on the other three issues. We should not settle here: there is clear headroom to extract a larger tranche and/or a lower out-of-quota rate before treating this as final. However, the direction of travel is good and a deal by round 3 or 4 looks plausible if they move substantially on tonnage.

instruction: Strong round. We've banked the two structural wins - country-specific allocation and a full, non-precedential UK carve-out from TCA disapplication - and we should say so plainly to keep momentum, but we now need to close the gap on the two numbers that actually matter: tranche size and the out-of-quota rate. Move as follows. First, reframe the ask: move our counter from 1.6m/2.4m total down to a UK tranche of 1.2 million tonnes within a total pool of around 1.8 million tonnes. Present this explicitly as a further UK concession from our round 2 position, made because they've now delivered fully on TCA and allocation - make clear that concession is contingent on real movement from them, not unilateral. Second, on the out-of-quota rate: hold hard against 50%, but signal we could land around 25-30% if tranche size moves substantially - frame the rate and the tranche as a single package, not separable asks. Third, on the review clause: tell them a purely procedural 18-month check is not sufficient given the size of the gap between our positions - we need an automatic, data-triggered reopening of the tranche if UK trade share or EU import volumes move materially against the baseline (e.g., a defined percentage shift), not just consultation. Signal that if they want a smaller initial tranche than we're asking, a genuinely binding automatic trigger is the only thing that could justify us accepting less up front - be clear this is a possible trade, not a concession yet made. Fourth - and only if needed to unlock real movement on tranche/rate - you now have authority to float, conditionally and explicitly, that the UK would be prepared to table improved country-specific quota treatment for EU exporters under our own safeguard measure as part of an overall package, IF the EU moves to a UK tranche in the 900,000 tonnes-1.2 million tonnes range with an out-of-quota rate at or below 30%. Do not make this a firm offer or put a number on the safeguard side yet - flag it as a signal of good faith and a sign we're serious about landing a durable deal, and gauge their reaction. Keep tone firm but constructive: acknowledge their movement, but be direct that 260,000 tonnes at 50% out-of-quota, even with TCA preserved, still pushes the large majority of UK trade onto a prohibitive rate, and that is not yet a modification we can accept as substantially equivalent. We have two rounds left after this one - signal we want to converge by round 4, not drag it out, but the current gap is still too wide to call this close.

authority.notes: These are round 3 counter-figures, not final settlement numbers - present as a further UK move contingent on EU reciprocity, not a floor. Internal floor guidance (not for disclosure): given TCA preference has now been fully and durably preserved via the UK-specific carve-out, the hard tranche floor from round 2 (1.4-1.5m) can flex downward - Ministers will accept a UK tranche as low as approximately 1,000,000 tonnes IF the out-of-quota rate comes down to 30% or below AND there is a binding, automatically-triggered review mechanism (not merely procedural) tied to objective trade-share or import-volume thresholds. If the out-of-quota rate remains at or near 50%, the tranche floor reverts upward toward 1.4m+ and no safeguard-based trade should be offered. Do not go below 1,000,000 tonnes tranche under any package this round. The EU exporter safeguard-quota improvement may now be floated conditionally and explicitly (not just hinted) as a bridging offer, but must not be firmed up with numbers until the EU has moved on tranche/rate first - sequence matters, do not offer it before they respond. Automatic review trigger is now treated as a partial substitute for tranche size, not a replacement for reasonable convergence on the headline number - do not accept a token tranche purely on the promise of a future review.

response_to_requests.request: Confirmation of tranche floor and how rate movement substitutes for volume
response_to_requests.why: TCA preservation was secured essentially for free, which gives us room to flex the tranche floor down from 1.4-1.5m to around 1,000,000 tonnes, but only if the out-of-quota rate falls to 30% or below - the two are now explicitly linked as a package, not independent asks.

response_to_requests.why: A genuinely binding, data-triggered reopening mechanism can justify accepting a somewhat smaller initial tranche than our stated ask, but it is not a substitute for a reasonable headline number - we will not accept a token initial tranche (e.g., near the EU's 260,000t offer) purely on the promise of a future review, regardless of how strong the review mechanism is.

private_rationale: The EU conceded the two cheapest items (allocation structure, TCA carve-out) very quickly, which strongly suggests they had room to move on those and were testing whether we'd bank them as a full settlement. We should not let structural wins substitute for the economically material terms - volume and rate are where their steel lobby will actually feel pain, so that's where the real negotiation is. We have two rounds left; I'm moving our number down from the round 2 opening (1.6m/2.4m) to a more convergence-oriented 1.2m/1.8m to signal serious intent to land a deal, while keeping an internal floor (1.0m tranche, ≤30% rate, binding review) that we would accept if pushed to round 4. Floating the safeguard leverage conditionally now (rather than waiting to round 4) uses our remaining time pressure advantage without committing to specifics before seeing their next move. If the EU still refuses to move meaningfully on tranche/rate in round 3, that tells us round 4 will likely be the resolution point or we walk to no-deal, and I should prepare the Minister for that fallback conversation (retaliation options, subsidy package) in parallel.

reasoning: No convergence yet. The EU's round 2 offer (550k pool/260k UK tranche/50% rate/procedural review) and the UK's round 2 counter (2.4mt pool/1.6mt tranche/25% rate/automatic trigger review) remain far apart on volume, rate, and review mechanism, even though allocation method and the TCA carve-out are now effectively settled. Per capital instructions, there is authorised headroom (up to 850k/450k/40% with a hybrid review mechanism) to test for a landing zone in round 3 before any decision to accept a deal or let the default apply. Accepting now would either lock in terms the UK has explicitly rejected as unworkable or abandon unused negotiating room; accepting default now would be premature given genuine movement on both sides and time remaining before the round 4 deadline.

The EU's round 2 offer (260,000t UK tranche within a 550,000t pool, 50% out-of-quota rate unchanged, 3 years with only a procedural 18-month review) falls far short of our authorised floor of a ~1,000,000t tranche with an out-of-quota rate at or below 30% and a binding, data-triggered review mechanism. While the EU has conceded the two structural points we prioritised most - country-specific allocation and a full, non-precedential TCA carve-out - they have not moved at all on the two numbers that actually determine real-world impact: tranche volume and out-of-quota rate. Accepting now would leave the overwhelming majority of UK trade exposed to a prohibitive 50% rate, which is not a genuine modification but a de facto withdrawal of the concession. There is clear evidence of EU flexibility elsewhere and time remaining (two rounds left) to converge on a workable package. I am continuing to press for a larger tranche, a materially lower out-of-quota rate, and a binding automatic review trigger, with the conditional safeguard-quota offer held in reserve as bridging leverage.

public_message: Thank you for engaging seriously with the structural elements — we'll treat the country-specific allocation method and the UK-specific TCA carve-out, with rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention conditions, as settled between us going forward; we won't reopen those, and we don't expect you to either. On the live issues, we are moving substantially further. First, volume: we can move the total pool from 550,000 to 850,000 tonnes, with the UK tranche rising from 260,000 to 450,000 tonnes — nearly double our last offer, and a significant step beyond an 11% figure toward roughly 19% of your historic trade as tariff-free access. Second, the rate: we can move from 50% to 40% out-of-quota, and we want to be clear this movement is linked to the volume movement — a package, not two separate asks. Third, on review: we propose a mandatory review at eighteen months with defined, objective triggers — UK trade share or EU import volume moving materially against baseline — which creates a presumption of adjustment and a binding obligation to renegotiate in good faith. That is a real mechanism with teeth, though we stop short of an automatic, self-executing reopening of the tranche, which we don't think either side's internal processes could sustain. We think this is a serious, substantial package — 850,000/450,000/40% together represents real movement on every axis you've raised. We need to be candid: your figures of a 1.6 million tonne tranche within a 2.4 million tonne pool at 25% out-of-quota are not something we can bring back to Council, and continuing to hold at that level risks us talking past each other into round 4 with no landing zone. Given our June timeline, we need your genuine counter-number now, not a restatement of your opening ask — where can you actually move to meet this?

UK-specific carve-out from FTA-disapplication text treated as settled, conditioned on rules-of-origin verification and anti-circumvention provisions, explicitly non-precedential for other FTA partners

18-month mandatory review with objective, pre-defined triggers (UK trade share or EU import volume movement against baseline) creating a presumption of adjustment and binding good-faith renegotiation obligation, but not an automatic self-executing reopening of tranche size

private_rationale: Following Brussels' authority exactly: 850k/450k/40%, hybrid review, allocation and TCA carve-out locked in as settled. Retaining the 250-300k pool / 100-150k tranche headroom and the 35% rate floor undisclosed for round 4, as instructed. Framing this as a large, credible move (doubling the round 2 figures) while explicitly rejecting UK's 1.6mt/2.4mt/25% as unworkable, to test whether they have a realistic floor closer to our range or are anchoring hard. Locking in the settled items reduces risk of re-litigation and protects the Japan/Korea non-precedent framing. Holding back headroom for round 4 preserves negotiating room in case UK moves meaningfully, while the explicit request for their 'real counter-number' is designed to force disclosure of their actual floor before we commit further capital-authorised movement in the final round given the June deadline pressure.

public_message: We recognise that is a further, real move on your part, and I want to acknowledge that the trajectory across three rounds has been constructive: allocation method and TCA treatment are now settled as far as we're concerned, and you've nearly doubled the tranche and moved ten points on the rate. But 450,000 tonnes is still under a fifth of our historic trade, and 40% out-of-quota on the remaining four-fifths is still, in practical terms, a rate designed to exclude rather than manage trade. We are prepared to move substantially to meet you, and will do so now rather than restate our round 2 position. We can come down from our 1.6 million tonne ask to a UK tranche of 1,000,000 tonnes, within a total pool of around 1,400,000 tonnes — a very significant concession from our side, more than a third off our last figure. In exchange, we need the out-of-quota rate at 30%, not 40%, and we need the review mechanism to have real teeth: an automatically triggered reopening of the tranche — not merely a presumption or a binding obligation to negotiate in good faith — where the defined trade-share or import-volume thresholds are met. We think a mechanism that requires us to renegotiate from scratch every time the data moves against us isn't durable; an automatic adjustment is what makes a three-year term workable without returning to Article XXVIII again in eighteen months' time. On duration, three years with that trigger at eighteen months is acceptable in principle. I'll also say plainly, since we're now trying to find the actual landing zone rather than trade further symbolic moves: if a package along these lines — 1,000,000 tonne tranche, 30% out-of-quota, automatic review trigger — is one Council could take back, we are prepared to табле, in parallel and as part of the same overall settlement, an improved country-specific quota allocation for EU exporters under the UK's own safeguard measure. That is a real offer, not a hint, and it reflects that we want a durable bilateral outcome, not just a formal box-ticking exercise on either side. We have one round left after this to close this properly — we'd rather use it to finalise detail than to keep moving headline numbers past each other.
