private_rationale: The EU has moved meaningfully on all three live axes (pool, tranche, rate) and explicitly asked for our real counter, signalling they want to converge this round or next given their June deadline. Sticking rigidly to 1.2m/1.8m/28% risks stalling momentum when they've shown clear willingness to keep moving; but caving toward their 450k/40% would breach our floor (1.0m tranche minimum, ≤30% rate, automatic trigger required) and undersell the leverage we still hold given their time pressure and our principal supplying interest. report: Round 3 concluded with a substantial UK move. We tabled our authorised package (850,000t total pool / 450,000t UK tranche / 40% out-of-quota / 3-year duration with an 18-month review carrying objective triggers and a binding good-faith renegotiation obligation, not automatic reopening), and explicitly locked in the allocation method and UK-specific TCA carve-out as settled, non-reversible, and non-precedential — the UK confirmed the same. On the live variables, the UK moved meaningfully off their round 2 position: from a 1.6m tonne tranche / 2.4m pool to a 1,000,000 tonne tranche within a 1,400,000 tonne total pool, while asking for 30% out-of-quota (down from their ask of 25%, up from our 40%) and insisting on an automatically triggered reopening of the tranche (not our presumption-plus-negotiate-in-good-faith model) tied to the same objective thresholds. They accepted 3-year duration with an 18-month trigger point in principle. Significantly, they also offered — explicitly framed as a real offer, not a hint — to improve the country-specific quota allocation for EU exporters under the UK's own steel safeguard, in parallel and as part of the same overall settlement. This is the first time they've put something from their side of the ledger on the table rather than only asking us to move. They flagged this is their real landing-zone offer and that they want to use round 4 to finalise detail rather than keep trading headline numbers.

recommendation.reasoning: A gap remains — UK at 1,000,000t tranche/1,400,000t pool/30%/automatic trigger versus our authorised 450,000t/850,000t/40%/presumption-based review. But the trajectory across three rounds shows genuine, specific, trade-anchored movement on both sides, not positional theatre, and the UK's offer to improve EU exporter treatment under their own safeguard is new, valuable, and directly responsive to one of our listed matters on the table (treatment of EU exporters under the UK measure) — it should be treated as real compensation flowing back to us, which changes the calculus on how far we can move on tranche/rate. This is the final round: we should use our full remaining headroom (pool to ~1.1m, tranche to ~600k, rate to 35%) as a genuine closing offer, explicitly conditioned on the UK confirming and formalising the reciprocal safeguard-quota improvement for EU exporters. On the automatic trigger, I recommend exploring a middle design — an automatic review (not automatic reopening) that obliges an expedited, time-bound renegotiation with a default fallback adjustment formula if talks fail within a fixed window (e.g. 60 days) — as a way to give the UK's 'teeth' concern real substance without fully ceding Council control over final tranche numbers. If the UK will not move materially off 1,000,000t/30% even against the safeguard linkage, we should be prepared to hold at our ceiling and accept that no settlement is reached in round 4, protecting the 40%/850k position as safer for Council approval, and let the six-month retaliation window run rather than concede terms Council cannot defend against Turkey/Korea comparators.

That is a very substantial move from our notified position — nearly triple the original pool, a tranche two-and-a-half times our round 2 offer, and fifteen points off the original rate. Duration remains three years, with allocation method and the UK-specific TCA carve-out — conditioned on rules-of-origin and anti-circumvention safeguards, and explicitly non-precedential for other principal suppliers — treated as settled, as we agreed last round. On the review mechanism, we can meet your concern about a toothless clause without a fully self-executing reopening: we propose that when the defined trade-share or import-volume thresholds are breached, it automatically triggers a mandatory renegotiation within a fixed sixty-day window, and if that window lapses without agreement, a pre-agreed default adjustment formula applies. That gives you a guaranteed outcome within a bounded timeframe, not an indefinite consultation, while keeping the substantive number subject to negotiation or a known formula rather than a unilateral shift. Finally, on your offer regarding EU exporters under your own safeguard — we take that seriously and want to build on it, but for this to be part of the same settlement, we need it specified and cross-referenced in the same instrument: which EU exporters, what quota improvement, what duration. A general assurance won't be enough for us to bring this back to Council as balanced. If we can agree on 1,100,000/600,000/35% with the review design I've set out, and a concrete reciprocal commitment on the safeguard side, I believe we have a durable landing zone we can both defend at home. If we can't converge near this, I'd rather say so plainly now than leave ambiguity: this is as far as we can go, and we understand the alternative is proceeding on the notified terms with your retaliation rights running from that point. I'd rather close this well with you than walk away from it.

public_message: That is a serious and substantial package, and I want to acknowledge it as such: 1.1 million tonnes total, a 600,000-tonne UK tranche, 35% out-of-quota, and a review mechanism with a genuine binding outcome — mandatory renegotiation within a bounded window and a default adjustment formula if that lapses — meets the substance of what we asked for on the mechanism. We're close. Let me try to close the remaining gap rather than leave it open. We can accept your rate of 35% and your review design as the basis for settlement. On the tranche, we ask you to move the last step, from 600,000 to 650,000 tonnes within a correspondingly adjusted pool of around 1,150,000 tonnes — that is a modest final ask given the distance we've both already travelled, and it reflects the floor below which we cannot honestly say this is a modification rather than a substantial impairment of our access. To help you take that back to Council, I will specify the reciprocal offer on our safeguard now rather than leave it general: the UK is prepared to uplift the EU's country-specific quota allocation under our own steel safeguard by up to 300,000 tonnes, or roughly a 20% increase on your current allocation, for a matching duration, cross-referenced in the same instrument as this settlement. If you can meet us at 650,000 tonnes on the tranche, we believe we have a package both sides can defend at home today. If 600,000 is genuinely immovable, we need to know that plainly now, because a 50,000-tonne gap is not a reason to walk away from a deal of this size — but we'd rather resolve it explicitly than assume it away.

report: Round 4 at the table: we tabled our authorised ceiling — 1,100,000t total pool, 600,000t UK-specific tranche, 35% out-of-quota rate, 3-year duration, allocation method and TCA carve-out confirmed as settled and non-precedential, and the hybrid review mechanism (automatic trigger to a mandatory 60-day renegotiation window, with a pre-agreed default adjustment formula applying only if that window lapses). We were explicit that this was our ceiling and that we would rather revert to the notified terms than exceed it without a concrete reciprocal commitment. The UK accepted the 35% rate outright and accepted our review mechanism design as meeting their 'teeth' concern in full — no further argument on either of those two points. They also, unprompted, specified their reciprocal offer in concrete terms rather than leaving it as a gesture: an uplift of up to 300,000 tonnes (~20% increase) to the EU's country-specific quota allocation under the UK's own steel safeguard, for a matching duration, cross-referenced in the same instrument. Their sole remaining ask is a final, modest increase on volume — tranche from 600,000 to 650,000 tonnes, pool from 1,100,000 to 1,150,000 tonnes (a ~4.5% move on each). They framed this explicitly as their true floor and asked for a plain answer rather than further rounds, noting there is no round 5.

recommendation.reasoning: This is a 50,000-tonne gap (4.5%) on pool and tranche beyond our explicit ceiling of 1,100,000/600,000, but every other element the UK has accepted in full: the 35% rate we wanted, our hybrid review design exactly as proposed (no self-executing automatic reopening — bounded renegotiation window plus default formula only as backstop), the 3-year duration, and the allocation method and TCA carve-out as settled and non-precedential. Critically, they have also converted their round 3 reciprocal offer into a specified, concrete commitment — a 300,000-tonne (~20%) uplift to the EU's own safeguard allocation for a matching duration, cross-referenced in the same instrument — which is exactly the level of specificity Brussels required before treating it as real compensation flowing back to us. Rejecting a deal of this scale over a 50,000-tonne increment (roughly 2% of the UK's historic trade) risks the six-month retaliation clock, hands Japan and Korea a live grievance to rally the UK around on FTA disapplication generally, and forfeits a concrete, quantified improvement to our own exporters' safeguard treatment that we would otherwise have to negotiate separately and with less leverage. The marginal cost of closing here is small; the marginal value of certainty, the reciprocal commitment, and avoiding an escalatory six-month window is large. I recommend capital authorise this final step to close now rather than hold at 600,000/1,100,000 and let the round lapse without settlement over a gap this narrow.

report: Final round closed with the EU tabling what they explicitly called their ceiling: total pool 1,100,000 tonnes, UK-specific tranche 600,000 tonnes, out-of-quota rate 35%, three-year duration, allocation method and TCA carve-out settled as previously agreed (non-precedential, conditioned on rules-of-origin/anti-circumvention), and a review mechanism with real teeth — automatic trigger on defined trade-share/import-volume thresholds leading to mandatory renegotiation within a 60-day window, with a pre-agreed default adjustment formula applying if that window lapses without agreement. This meets our mechanism requirement (self-executing outcome, not pure good-faith renegotiation) and lands within one of our two preferred review formulations. I pushed for one further step — tranche to 650,000t within a 1,150,000t pool — and formalised the safeguard reciprocity offer with actual numbers (up to 300,000 tonnes / ~20% uplift to the EU's quota allocation under our own safeguard, matching duration, cross-referenced in the same instrument) to help them justify the final move to Council. The EU has not yet confirmed whether they can stretch to 650,000t; they were explicit this was their ceiling, but did not walk away when I pushed for the extra 50,000 tonnes, and left the door open by asking for the safeguard specifics, which I have now supplied. There is no further round after this one. The gap remaining, if the EU holds firm, is 50,000 tonnes on the tranche (600k vs our 650k ask) and a correspondingly smaller total pool — everything else (rate, review design, duration, TCA carve-out, allocation method, safeguard reciprocity) is aligned or resolved.

recommendation.reasoning: This is the final round; there is no round 5 to extract further concessions, and the EU stated plainly and credibly that 1,100,000/600,000/35% is their ceiling, consistent with a pattern of real, substantial movement every round (from 400k/FCFS/50% with no review to a ring-fenced country-specific tranche, full TCA carve-out, 35% rate, and a genuinely self-executing review mechanism with a bounded timeframe and default formula). The 600,000-tonne tranche is only 50,000 tonnes short of our authorised floor of 650,000, and the review mechanism offered is strong enough to substitute for some of that shortfall — it guarantees an outcome (default adjustment formula) rather than leaving us dependent on future goodwill. Walking away over a 50,000-tonne gap risks reverting to the notified terms (400,000t global FCFS, 50% out-of-quota, no review, TCA disapplication) which is categorically worse on every metric, and would only be recoverable via a six-month-delayed retaliation that carries its own economic and political costs and does not restore lost UK export volume in the interim. The package as a whole — allocation method won, TCA preference preserved via a durable non-precedential carve-out, tranche more than doubled from opening EU position, rate down 15 points, and a review mechanism with real bite — represents a materially different outcome from the opening anchor and is defensible as 'substantially equivalent' compensation in the round 4 context, especially paired with the safeguard reciprocity we are offering. I recommend Ministers accept these terms if the EU will not move the final 50,000 tonnes, rather than let the process lapse with no agreement at all on the table.
